extracted.intended_audience: citizens, lawmakers, and constitution framers interested in designing or evaluating republican constitutions and separation-of-powers arrangements
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and practical criteria for structuring a republican government so as to maintain separation of powers while providing effective constitutional checks among legislative, executive, and judicial departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of the three departments ('separate and distinct')
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative, executive, and judiciary departments ought to be 'separate and distinct' so that 'neither exercise the powers properly belonging to the other; nor shall any person exercise the powers of more than one of them at the same time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the fundamental maxim: avoid intermixture and consolidation of powers. The text cites state constitutions that declare this rule and then documents how in practice many offices and powers have been blended (appointments by other departments, members holding multiple offices). Caveat: the maxim does not demand absolute isolation if practical considerations require certain overlaps (e.g., judiciary qualifications or tenure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual constitutional control: checks must exist between departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments should be connected and blended enough to give each a constitutional control over the others; complete, isolated separation prevents effective constitutional restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues that if departments are too far separated they cannot check encroachments. The correct structure supplies constitutional means (not just paper boundaries) so each department can 'effectually check and restrain' the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior structural safeguards over 'parchment barriers'
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere demarcation in the written constitution (a 'parchment barrier') is insufficient; practical defenses are indispensably necessary to prevent encroachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience shows written limits are often over-rated. The constitution must 'contrive the interior structure of the government' so constituent parts, by their mutual relations, keep one another in proper places (e.g., appointment methods, tenure, blended powers that create mutual dependence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent legislative predominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and counteract the natural tendency of the legislative department to extend its sphere and aggrandize itself at the expense of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include: legislative powers are more extensive and less precisely limited, legislatures control public money and rewards, and are more able to mask encroachments under complex measures. Design provisions should specifically aim to prevent legislative usurpation (examples and evidence drawn from Virginia and Pennsylvania).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment independence (minimize cross-appointment influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of each department should have as little agency as possible in the appointment of members of the others; ideally appointments derive from the people by separate channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appointments are intermingled (legislature appointing executives/judges, executive appointing judges with legislative influence), dependence fosters encroachment. The recommendation is to draw appointments from the same fountain (the people) but through independent channels to give each department 'a will of its own.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial independence of officeholders (independence in emoluments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of each department should be as little dependent as possible on the others for salaries and emoluments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If, for example, judges or executives rely on the legislature for pay, their nominal independence is undermined and the legislature can exert undue influence. Fixing judicial salaries and insulating emoluments are practical safeguards cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial safeguards: permanent tenure and qualification-focused selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial appointments may justify some deviation from rigid appointment-separation because of the need to secure peculiar qualifications and the stabilizing effect of permanent tenure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because judges require special qualifications and permanent tenure tends to destroy dependence on the appointing authority, strict application of appointment-separation can be relaxed in favor of selecting methods that best secure judicial competence and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structural incentives: 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition'
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the constitution so that the personal motives and constitutional means available to officeholders create mutual resistance to encroachments — i.e., ambition of each department checks ambition of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'interest of the man must be connected with the constitutional rights of the place.' Provide each department with the constitutional means and personal motives to resist invasions of its rights (examples: vetoes, appointment checks, staggered terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about appeals to the people (occasional or periodical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional or periodical appeals to the people (conventions, councils, periodic revisions) are an inadequate and sometimes harmful remedy for department encroachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections: appeals may fail when two departments combine; frequent appeals erode reverence for government; appeals inflame public passions and party influence, producing decisions swayed by passions not reason; conventions are often composed of those with partisan connection to the issues. Historical examples (Jefferson's draught, Council of Censors, Pennsylvania experience) illustrate these pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of censorial/revisory bodies (Council of Censors example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies created to inquire and censure constitutional violations (e.g., Pennsylvania's Council of Censors) are vulnerable to party division, partisan composition, and limited practical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Council of Censors was split into violent parties, often misinterpreted constitutional limits, and its decisions did not reliably alter legislative practice; thus such bodies may demonstrate the disease but be an inefficient cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural precautions to restrain legislative abuse (e.g., pre-publication of bills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural requirements, such as that all public bills be previously printed for consideration by the people, are constitutional precautions against improper legislative acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes many laws violated the rule requiring prior printing of bills — highlighting the importance of embedding and enforcing such procedural safeguards to prevent hasty or clandestine legislative encroachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve judiciary jurisdiction and trial by jury from legislative encroachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional guarantees such as the trial by jury and the proper assignment of cases to judiciary determination must be preserved from being drawn into legislative cognizance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Pennsylvania show legislatures sometimes assumed judicial powers, varied judges' salaries, and drew judicial cases within legislative determination; these are cited as violations that constitutional design should prevent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper allocation of executive prerogatives (avoid vesting executive functions in legislature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive prerogatives (such as pardon) should be vested in the executive department and not transferred to the legislative department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State constitutions are cited where legislature exercises appointment and pardon powers, contributing to consolidation; constitutional design should allocate core executive functions to the executive to maintain balance.
